title: <a download>: browsers navigate instead of downloading when the href, or a redirect, is cross-origin
body:
Below follows a bot analysis of why all the major browsers convert a download that got redirected to a cross origin into a navigation, sort of. This should probably be spec'ed?

### What is the issue with the HTML Standard?

[Download the hyperlink](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/links.html#downloading-hyperlinks) fetches the URL with the default redirect mode ("follow") and passes the final response to [handle as a download](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/links.html#handle-as-a-download). The algorithm never checks origins and never navigates. The only cross-origin mitigation is in [get the suggested filename](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/links.html#getting-the-suggested-filename), which drops the `download` attribute's filename. Step 7 lets the user agent return, which does nothing. It does not let the user agent navigate.

All three engines do something else. When the link's URL is cross-origin, or a redirect takes the fetch cross-origin, they drop the download and navigate the link's navigable to that URL instead.

**Case 1: `href` is cross-origin.** This is #2562, which is still open. Every engine now ignores the `download` attribute and follows the link as an ordinary hyperlink:

- Gecko: [`nsContentUtils::TriggerLink`](https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/rev/a82bcf39e8d23e7b06e021044db52f74210862ce/dom/base/nsContentUtils.cpp#7658) ("For security reasons we only allow websites to declare same-origin resources as downloadable. If this check fails we will just do the normal thing (i.e. navigate to the resource).")
- WebKit: `parseDownloadAttribute` in `Source/WebCore/html/AnchorElementFunctions.cpp` ("The download attribute on anchor was ignored because its href URL has a different security origin.")
- Chromium: [issue 40516916](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40516916) (formerly crbug.com/714373), shipped in Chrome 65 ([chromestatus](https://chromestatus.com/feature/4969697975992320), [intent](https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/Iw3_SUcagGg)): "To avoid what is essentially user-mediated cross-origin information leakage".

**Case 2: `href` is same-origin but redirects cross-origin.** For example, `<a download href="/r">` where `/r` returns a 302 to `https://other.example/page.html`, which serves `text/html` without `Content-Disposition`. The spec says the page is saved and the frame keeps its document. In every engine the download is dropped and the frame navigates to the redirect target, so the page is rendered:

- Gecko: [`HttpBaseChannel::SetupReplacementChannel`](https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/rev/a82bcf39e8d23e7b06e021044db52f74210862ce/netwerk/protocol/http/HttpBaseChannel.cpp#5343) copies the attachment hint to the redirected channel only when the new URL is same-origin with the original one. Without the hint the response is handled as a document.
- WebKit: [`PendingDownload::willSendRedirectedRequest`](https://searchfox.org/wubkat/rev/549bd1fb46a60fc3d27f30d7cf32fc04611d73a3/Source/WebKit/NetworkProcess/Downloads/PendingDownload.cpp#116-140) cancels the download on a cross-origin redirect. It then [loads the redirect target in the frame](https://searchfox.org/wubkat/rev/549bd1fb46a60fc3d27f30d7cf32fc04611d73a3/Source/WebKit/WebProcess/Network/NetworkProcessConnection.cpp#346-355). This was added in 2024 as a security fix: "Block cross origin redirect downloads in iframe" ([284937@main](https://commits.webkit.org/284937@main)), followed by "For Blocked cross origin redirect downloads, try rendering the page instead" ([285050@main](https://commits.webkit.org/285050@main)). The first commit message gives the motivation: "This could lead to attacker controlled javascript get access to cross origin cookies which should not be."
- Chromium: drops the download at the cross-origin redirect and starts a navigation to the redirect target.

All three engines compare origins, not sites, so a cross-origin same-site redirect also navigates. Same-origin redirects are still downloaded everywhere.

All three engines did this deliberately, for security reasons. I think the spec should be changed to match.

### Why engines do this

The threat is the one the warning in [get the suggested filename](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/links.html#getting-the-suggested-filename) describes. It was set out when Gecko first implemented `download` ([Mozilla bug 676619 comment 20](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=676619#c20), [comment 15](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=676619#c15)). Suppose `evil.example` contains `<a download="cat.jpg" href="https://bank.example/statement">`. One click makes the browser fetch the statement with the user's `bank.example` cookies and write it to disk, with little sign of where it came from. The user can then be talked into uploading "the file they just downloaded" back to `evil.example`. A link without `download` can't do this: the response is rendered under `bank.example`'s origin, and the user would have to choose to save it. The forced download also persists responses that the server marked `no-store`.

The spec addresses this only by dropping the suggested filename. The engines instead refuse to force the download. Ignoring the filename doesn't stop the save itself, which is the part that matters.

Redirects need the same check. Otherwise the `href` check is trivial to get around: `evil.example` serves `<a download href="/r">`, where `/r` redirects to `https://bank.example/statement`. The `href` is same-origin, so it passes the check, and the spec would then save the bank's response. Checking the origin of every hop, not only the first, is what makes the `href` check mean anything.
